A smart pointer is a struct that owns data and implements Deref (so it behaves like a reference) and usually Drop (so it frees on scope exit). Rust has no garbage collector — these types give you the specific sharing and lifetime semantics you ask for.

The cast

Type Ownership Mutability Thread-safe Cost
Box<T> unique as inner if T: Send one allocation
Rc<T> shared, counted immutable only no counter ++/--
Arc<T> shared, atomic counted immutable only yes atomic ++/--
Cell<T> owns Copy in/out, no borrow no zero
RefCell<T> owns runtime-checked &mut no one flag
Mutex<T> owns runtime-locked &mut yes lock/unlock
RwLock<T> owns many readers / one writer yes lock/unlock
Cow<'a, T> borrowed or owned write-on-clone yes enum

Box<T>

Heap allocation with a single owner. Three real uses:

Box<dyn Error> is the classic "I don't care what the error type is" return:

Rc<T> — shared ownership, single thread

Rc::clone is idiomatic — writing it that way signals "this is a reference-count bump, not a deep copy".

Gotcha: Rc<T> gives shared immutable access only. To mutate you need Rc<RefCell<T>>. And Rc is not Send — using it across threads is a compile error, which is exactly the protection you want.

Reference cycles leak

Break cycles with Weak<T>:

Weak::upgrade returns Option<Rc<T>> — None if the value has been dropped.

Arc<T> — shared ownership across threads

Arc costs one atomic increment per clone, which is ~10–20× more expensive than Rc's plain increment. Use Rc when you are single-threaded.

Interior mutability: Cell and RefCell

Sometimes you need to mutate through a &T. The borrow checker cannot see that your usage is safe, so Cell/RefCell move the check to runtime.

Cell<T> — copy in, copy out

Zero runtime cost — Cell just allows the write. Works for Copy types (or replace/take for others). No references into the cell, which is why it is free.

RefCell<T> — runtime-checked borrows

The panic message is already borrowed: BorrowMutError (or already mutably borrowed: BorrowError). Try try_borrow / try_borrow_mut for a Result instead of a panic.

The Rc<RefCell<T>> idiom

Shared and mutable, single thread. This is what a graph, an observer list, or a DOM-like tree looks like in Rust.

Gotcha: holding a borrow() across a call that also borrows mutably is the classic RefCell panic. Collect into a Vec first, or drop the guard explicitly (drop(guard)) before recursing.

Mutex and RwLock

lock() returns a MutexGuard — a RAII lock that releases on drop. It also gives you &mut T, which is how Mutex provides mutation.

Mutex poisoning

If a thread panics while holding the lock, the mutex is poisoned and every later lock() returns Err. .unwrap() then cascades the panic.

RwLock vs Mutex

Use RwLock when reads vastly outnumber writes and the critical section is long enough for contention to matter. For short critical sections, Mutex is usually faster (no reader-counting overhead). Measure.

Atomics

For counters and flags, atomics beat a mutex by a wide margin.

Ordering Guarantee Use
Relaxed atomicity only counters, stats
Acquire / Release pairs: a load sees everything before the matching store flags, handoff
SeqCst total order across all threads when in doubt

Rule of thumb: Relaxed for statistics, Acquire/Release for publication of data, SeqCst only if you cannot reason about it.

Cow<'a, T> — clone on write

Ideal for "usually no change" transformations: config parsing, HTML escaping, path normalisation. Used heavily by serde and regex.

Choosing, in one table

Need Use
Recursive type or trait object Box<T>
Share read-only, one thread Rc<T>
Share read-only, many threads Arc<T>
Mutate through &self, one thread, Copy data Cell<T>
Mutate through &self, one thread, complex data RefCell<T>
Mutate through &self, many threads Mutex<T> / RwLock<T>
Simple counter/flag, many threads Atomic*
Usually borrowed, sometimes owned Cow<'a, T>
Global config, init once OnceLock<T> / LazyLock<T>

Rule of thumb: if your design needs Rc<RefCell<...>> in three places, the data model is probably wrong. Re-read module 02.03 and ask who really owns what. Interior mutability is a scalpel, not a general-purpose tool.

A worked example: a shared cache with Arc<RwLock<HashMap>>

#[derive(Clone)] on a struct holding an Arc clones the handle, not the data. That is why cache.clone() is safe and free to pass into threads.

Exercises

  1. Write a recursive Tree enum using Box and a depth() method.
  2. Convert an Rc<RefCell<T>> linked list to use Weak for the back-pointer and prove the cycle is broken by printing Rc::strong_count.
  3. Implement a thread-safe counter three ways — Mutex<u64>, AtomicU64, and RwLock<u64> — and benchmark 8 threads × 1M increments.
  4. Write fn sanitise(s: &str) -> Cow<'_, str> that strips control characters. Assert it borrows for clean input.
  5. Build a LazyLock<HashMap<&str, &str>> for a static lookup table.
  6. Explain why Rc<T> cannot be sent to another thread, and what the compiler error says.
